courses.title: 1. C/C++ foundations for trustworthy computation
courses.summary: Build a native numerical program, manage memory safely, and establish a correctness oracle before making it faster. Explore how floating-point order changes an answer.
outcomes: Compile and test C17 and C++17 programs with explicit input bounds.
Explain contiguous storage, ownership, integer range and floating-point rounding.
Choose an independent reference and a justified error tolerance.

lessons.title: A native workflow and a precise problem
paragraphs: HPC begins with a workload and a definition of a correct answer. A numerical kernel may run on one core, many CPU cores, multiple nodes, or accelerators. Start here with command-line programs on a development computer. Install a C/C++ compiler and a terminal; Linux or WSL is convenient, and macOS supports these examples with the noted runtime requirements. Use C17 for the C version or C++17 for the C++ version. These are host programs with main(), not Arduino setup()/loop() sketches.

Build a debug executable with warnings and address/undefined-behavior instrumentation, run small cases, then make a separate optimized build. Record compiler name, version, flags, input size and expected output. Change one thing at a time. The browser experiment evaluates a bounded numerical model, while the source editor provides a standalone native program you can edit, download and compile. A browser result does not certify an edited native program; run its own tests after every edit.
lessons.pitfall: Do not compare a sanitized debug build against an optimized release build and attribute the entire difference to your algorithm.

lessons.title: Arrays, pointers and ownership
paragraphs: An array gives an index-to-address mapping. For doubles in these examples, element i occupies eight bytes and contiguous elements are adjacent. A pointer names an address; it carries neither a bounds check nor ownership. Pass the pointer together with a length, use indices strictly less than that length, initialize storage before reading it, and ensure multiplication used to size an allocation cannot overflow. The examples cap inputs before multiplying dimensions.

The C files use calloc and explicit free through BUFFER/RELEASE helpers. Their C++ equivalents use std::vector for initialized contiguous storage and automatic lifetime management. The pointer returned by data() is valid only while the vector storage remains alive and is not reallocated. Passing a vector by value copies its elements; prefer a const reference or a pointer-and-length view for a read-only kernel. Neither language makes a dangling pointer or out-of-bounds access valid.
lessons.pitfall: Growing a vector may invalidate pointers into it. Keep storage stable while a kernel or worker uses those pointers.

lessons.title: Integer and floating-point contracts
paragraphs: Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior in C and C++; a compiler need not preserve a wraparound result. Widen before multiplication: (long long)n * (n + 1) differs from casting an already-overflowed int product. Unsigned modular arithmetic is defined, but a wrapped allocation length is still incorrect. For floating-point work, addition rounds to the representable format, so changing the order of a reduction can change the answer.

The lab sums 100000000, n copies of 1, then -100000000. With a binary32 accumulator, each small addition can disappear next to the large value. The binary64 path exactly handles these bounded integers. Small-first ordering can help, but even it rounds when a total is not representable. For general scientific values, compare absolute error near zero and relative error at scale. Specify atol + rtol * abs(reference), reject non-finite outputs, and choose tolerances from the numerical problem.
lessons.pitfall: A faster result outside the numerical contract is a failed optimization, even if its checksum looks plausible.

lessons.title: Tests that can expose a wrong optimization
paragraphs: Use a simple trusted reference, a known analytical answer, or both. Check every output element when feasible; a checksum alone can hide canceling errors. Test a one-element input, odd lengths, lengths around a tile or vector boundary, zero values where allowed, negative inputs and a representative large problem. An unsupported zero-length input should be rejected cleanly rather than silently executing an invalid loop.

The native correctness example prints the float error but exits successfully only when its double result matches the integer reference. This distinction matters: an intentionally inaccurate demonstration should not be mistaken for a correct production algorithm. AddressSanitizer helps detect invalid memory accesses; UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer catches selected language violations. A clean sanitizer run covers only the executions tested and is not a proof that every future input is safe.
lessons.pitfall: Turning on fast-math can change NaN, infinity, signed-zero and reassociation behavior. Revisit the numerical contract before enabling it.

formulas.title: Mixed error tolerance

formulas.assumptions: Both values must be finite; tolerances come from the application.
formulas.example: For reference 100, atol 0.001 and rtol 0.0001, the allowed absolute error is 0.011.

formulas.assumptions: The product must fit size_t and the available memory.
formulas.example: One million eight-byte doubles occupy 8,000,000 bytes before other arrays or overhead.

options.text: Reject all differences regardless of the numerical contract
atol=0.001 and rtol=0.0001
atol=0 and rtol=0

courses.title: 2. Benchmarking and performance evidence
courses.summary: Measure repeated native runs, separate setup from kernel time, consume results, and interpret distributions instead of selecting one favorable number.
outcomes: Define a reproducible benchmark protocol.
Analyze warm-up, median, variability and speedup.
Distinguish algorithmic work, measured time and performance models.

lessons.title: Define what the clock includes
paragraphs: Write down whether you want kernel latency, complete application latency or throughput over a batch. Allocation, file I/O, initialization, thread creation, compilation and result checking may dominate a short calculation. A kernel benchmark normally initializes buffers before starting the clock and checks outputs after stopping it; an end-to-end benchmark includes the work the user actually waits for. Report both if their distinction changes the decision.

Use an elapsed monotonic clock. The C examples use clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC); C++ uses steady_clock; OpenMP and MPI examples use their runtime wall timers. CPU time accumulated across threads is not elapsed wall time. If a sample is near the clock’s resolution, increase the workload or repeat the kernel inside a sample while preserving its semantics. An apparent zero time is evidence of inadequate measurement, not infinite throughput.
lessons.pitfall: Comparing times with different input sizes, precision or included setup does not establish a fair speedup.

lessons.title: Make the measured work observable
paragraphs: An optimizing compiler can delete work whose result is never used. The companion program prints a checksum after every sample and checks it against the serial reference. It changes one input outside the timed region so repeated calls cannot simply reuse a prior result, and keeps kernel functions out of line for inspection. These techniques make this example useful, but you should still inspect generated code when measuring very small kernels.

The candidate uses two independent sums and then combines them, exposing a different dependency structure. For this bounded integer-valued dataset both sums are exactly representable in double. With general floating-point input, reassociation may change results, so the same transformation needs a tolerance-based test. Do not mark every element volatile to stop optimization: that changes the memory operations being benchmarked. Prefer observable outputs and a testable workload.
lessons.pitfall: A benchmark that accidentally measures only timer overhead can look stable while saying almost nothing about the kernel.

lessons.title: Warm-up, noise and paired comparisons
paragraphs: Run several samples and retain the raw data. A first run may fault in pages, initialize runtime state, or populate caches; decide in advance how many warm-up samples to exclude. Keep the same policy for baseline and candidate. The provided native harness alternates which implementation runs first to reduce a simple order bias. Record whether the data is intentionally cache-hot or cache-cold; those are different experiments.

Use the median as a robust descriptive center and show a range or quantiles so readers can see variability. A small median difference inside a broad overlapping distribution needs more investigation. Keep problem size, compiler flags, thread placement and machine power conditions fixed. On shared systems, background activity matters. A handful of samples and a speedup ratio do not by themselves establish statistical significance or portability to a different CPU.
lessons.pitfall: Discarding only the slow candidate samples after seeing the result is selection bias.

lessons.title: Find the expensive phase before rewriting it
paragraphs: Instrument meaningful phases first: preparation, transfer, compute, synchronization and output. Profile a representative input to locate the dominant work, then form a falsifiable hypothesis. For example, changing row traversal may reduce data movement; adding threads may reduce compute time but increase synchronization. Use a profiler or hardware counters on a supported host to test the mechanism, with the same build and input used in the benchmark.

The browser panel analyzes supplied timing samples. Its initial numbers are illustrative; replacing them with your native baseline_ms and candidate_ms columns turns it into an evidence worksheet. It does not run a compiler. Keep a result ledger with command, environment, correctness outcome, median and spread. If an optimization improves only a tiny phase, calculate its end-to-end impact before making code harder to maintain.
lessons.pitfall: Profiler overhead and debug instrumentation can alter timing. Collect correctness diagnostics and release timing as separate runs.

Native C++ measurements taken by this page
Your processor’s guaranteed latency

courses.title: 3. Memory locality and cache behavior
courses.summary: Connect C/C++ array layout to cache lines, working sets and traversal order. Measure real traversals and use a transparent cache model to explain a hypothesis.
outcomes: Derive row-major byte addresses.
Separate spatial locality, temporal reuse and capacity misses.
Design a cache experiment without treating simulated misses as hardware counters.

lessons.title: From indices to addresses
paragraphs: A flat N by N row-major array stores element (row,column) at row*N+column. With eight-byte elements, its byte offset is 8*(row*N+column). Advancing the inner column index by one accesses the next element; advancing the row index by one jumps by 8*N bytes. The C and C++ examples both use this layout. A vector of vectors is a different representation: its rows may be separately allocated, so do not assume one flat buffer.

In the native walk() function, only the index expression changes between row and column traversal. Both paths visit the same initialized values and compute the same sum. This makes it possible to test locality while preserving useful work. For large matrices, the strided path often fails to use all the data fetched in a line before eviction. Hardware prefetching and real cache organization affect the measured outcome, so predict a mechanism and then measure it.
lessons.pitfall: Changing storage layout and traversal simultaneously makes it harder to isolate the source of a speed difference.

lessons.title: Spatial locality and a stated cache model
paragraphs: A cache transfers groups of bytes called lines. With the teaching model set to 64-byte lines, eight adjacent doubles share a line. A cold row traversal of 1024 doubles needs 128 distinct lines; seven of each eight accesses can hit if the line stays resident. The explorer records actual addresses and runs them through a fully associative least-recently-used cache. Its capacity is entered in lines, not elements.

For a 32 by 32 matrix and a 16-line cache, a column pass revisits a row’s line only after touching many other lines. That reuse distance can exceed the capacity, causing repeated misses. A real processor has multiple cache levels, set associativity, prefetchers, replacement policies and other traffic. Its cache-line size is a property to measure or look up, not a portable constant. The explorer deliberately makes each simplifying assumption visible.
lessons.pitfall: A modeled miss is not a fixed number of nanoseconds; overlapping requests and memory-level parallelism can change elapsed cost.

lessons.title: Working set, reuse and data layout
paragraphs: Temporal locality means reusing a value while it is still nearby in the memory hierarchy. Compute the working set of every live array, not just the input you are looking at. Three 512 by 512 double matrices occupy 6,291,456 bytes, which may exceed a small private cache. Reusing a submatrix before moving on is one motivation for tiling. Moving an already resident line between cores introduces another issue: coherence, discussed in the threading courses.

Array-of-structures groups all fields of each record; structure-of-arrays groups one field across records. If a kernel reads only positions from a large particle record, separate position arrays can reduce unnecessary traffic and make SIMD access simpler. If it consumes every field per particle, a different layout may win. State the access pattern first, then compare layouts under the same memory footprint and numerical output contract.
lessons.pitfall: Padding every structure can inflate the working set enough to erase a hoped-for benefit.

lessons.title: Validate a locality hypothesis
paragraphs: Predict the distinct line count for one sequential pass, then change only traversal order. Vary the model capacity until a previously strided reuse fits. Observe that the checksum is invariant while cache counts change. Use a matrix small enough to inspect addresses by hand before moving to a larger native allocation. Test N=17 as well as powers of two so a convenient alignment does not hide a boundary bug.

The native program reports row_ms and column_ms over repeated samples. Its values are measured wall time, while the browser’s misses are model counts. Do not derive a real bandwidth from simulated bytes and native time without a justified memory-traffic model. A native profiler can collect relevant cache or memory events where available, but event definitions and permissions differ by machine. Preserve compiler flags, input size and traversal order in the notebook.
lessons.pitfall: A small cache-hot array can show little difference between traversals. That is a meaningful result for that working set.

formulas.assumptions: A flat array of eight-byte doubles with no per-row padding.
formulas.example: At N=32, (2,3) is element 67, offset 536 bytes.

Input values are small integers in double storage, so the sums are exactly representable at the supported limits.

practice.prompt: What is temporal locality?

options.text: Reusing data before it leaves the relevant memory level
Always reading a different row
Using the wall clock to order array elements

options.text: Column values are not initialized
Reuse distance exceeds the small cache’s capacity
It computes more additions than row traversal

options.text: Fully associative LRU replacement
The exact policy of your CPU
An infinite cache with no evictions

options.text: The number of cache misses in every configuration
The native elapsed time exactly
The sum of all elements

questions.explanation: Same data and arithmetic contract require equal useful results.

questions.prompt: A kernel reads only x positions from large particle records. Which layout is worth testing?

options.text: Copying all unused fields every iteration
A separate contiguous x array
Padding every particle to a page

questions.explanation: A structure-of-arrays layout can reduce unused data traffic for this access pattern.

questions.prompt: Can modeled cache misses be reported as your CPU’s measured cache misses?

options.text: No; collect native counters to make that claim
Yes, if the browser uses the same language
Yes, because all processors use LRU

questions.explanation: The model omits actual associativity, prefetching and other traffic.

courses.title: 4. Algorithms, loop order and cache tiling
courses.summary: Optimize dense matrix multiplication while preserving every output, including edge tiles. Understand why reducing data movement can matter more than removing an arithmetic operation.
outcomes: Count useful operations independently of source-line count.
Implement and test a tiled loop nest in C or C++.
Choose tile candidates from working-set estimates and measured evidence.

lessons.title: Count the work and choose the algorithm
paragraphs: For dense square multiplication C=A*B, each output C[i,j] is the sum over k of A[i,k]*B[k,j]. The conventional operation count is about 2*N^3 FLOPs: one multiply and one add for each triple. This convention counts an FMA as two arithmetic operations even when it is one machine instruction. Doubling N increases conventional work by roughly eight times and matrix storage by four times.

Before tuning loops, ask whether the task needs a dense matrix, whether structure such as sparsity can be used, and whether a tested numerical library already provides a better kernel. This course implements a small dense kernel to make the mechanisms inspectable. It is not a replacement for a vendor-tuned BLAS. An algorithmic reduction in work and a lower constant factor at the same complexity are different kinds of improvement.
lessons.pitfall: Comparing an optimized dense kernel with an incorrect or unnecessary computation is not a meaningful baseline.

lessons.title: Preserve dependence while changing traversal
paragraphs: The reference uses i-j-k order, computing one output at a time. The tiled candidate uses blocks in ii-kk-jj order and inner i-k-j order. For a fixed i and k, A[i,k] can be reused while j walks contiguous B and C entries. The k contributions for each output still arrive in increasing order in this implementation. Moving loops is legal only when data dependencies and observable behavior allow it.

Initialize C to zero before accumulating into it. If a benchmark calls an accumulating kernel repeatedly without resetting C, the candidate computes a different problem on later samples. Input A and B must remain unchanged while outputs are built. Overlapping input and output buffers can introduce dependencies absent from the mathematical operation. State a non-overlap requirement or deliberately handle overlap; do not simply assume it because a pointer is const.
lessons.pitfall: const prevents writes through that pointer; it does not prove that another pointer cannot alias the same memory.

lessons.title: Tile size and partial edges
paragraphs: A rough working-set estimate for three B by B double tiles is 3*B*B*8 bytes. It helps choose a starting range, but usable cache capacity is smaller than the headline total and other data or associativity may interfere. Register blocking, packing and vectorization make real library kernels more sophisticated than this teaching implementation. Sweep several tile sizes rather than treating one cache calculation as an optimality proof.

When N is not divisible by B, the last tile is partial. Each inner loop must stop at min(block_start+B,N). Test a tile larger than the matrix and a one-element tile as well as a non-divisible size. The browser computes both actual matrices and compares every element; its optional cache trace applies a stated LRU model. A lower modeled miss count supports a locality hypothesis but does not guarantee a native speedup.
lessons.pitfall: Writing a full B by B edge tile without clipping accesses memory beyond the array.

lessons.title: A reproducible optimization experiment
paragraphs: Run N=17 with tile 8, N=33 with tile 7, and N=7 with tile 32. The expected maximum error is zero for the small integer inputs used here. Then use non-integer data and a justified tolerance to investigate floating-point sensitivity. Keep an independent reference after optimizing; testing a candidate against an identical copy of itself proves little.

The native companion prints one baseline and tiled wall time plus the maximum element error. Treat a single time as an observation; repeat the command or extend it to a sample loop with a defined warm-up policy before drawing a performance conclusion. Include C initialization consistently in the reported scope. Compare the same compiler flags and data, then inspect reports or a profiler to explain what changed.
lessons.pitfall: A checksum match does not certify edge tiles. The verification must examine the whole matrix.

formulas.symbols: N is square matrix width; FLOPs counts multiply and add separately.
formulas.assumptions: Conventional dense algorithm; ignore lower-order initialization work.

formulas.assumptions: A rough capacity estimate, not a complete register/cache model.

The native algorithm can retain values in registers; the browser trace intentionally counts explicit accesses instead of claiming to reconstruct compiler output.

courses.title: 5. SIMD and compiler vectorization
courses.summary: Expose independent iterations, inspect compiler decisions, and handle vector tails correctly. Connect vectorization to data layout and numerical semantics.
outcomes: Distinguish SIMD lanes from threads.
Use compiler reports to investigate vectorized and missed loops.
Test remainders, overlap assumptions and floating-point contracts.

lessons.title: One operation across multiple elements
paragraphs: SIMD applies an instruction to several data lanes. It is distinct from adding operating-system threads: one thread can use a vector unit, and many threads may each vectorize their inner loops. The AXPY-style kernel here computes out[i]=2*x[i]+y[i]. Each output is independent if the input and output arrays satisfy the stated non-overlap conditions. That makes it a good starting loop for compiler vectorization.

Lane count depends on instruction-set width and element type, and some architectures support scalable vectors. A model with four lanes illustrates grouping without promising a particular instruction sequence. The browser computes groups and a remainder using ordinary bounded operations. For native evidence, compile with optimization and inspect the compiler report or assembly. Source-level grouping alone does not prove that machine SIMD instructions were emitted.
lessons.pitfall: Four lanes do not imply exactly four times the end-to-end speed: memory traffic, dependencies, setup and tails still cost time.

lessons.title: Ask the compiler what happened
paragraphs: With Clang, add -Rpass=loop-vectorize, -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize and -Rpass-analysis=loop-vectorize to a release compilation. With GCC, use -fopt-info-vec-optimized and -fopt-info-vec-missed. Read the message for the target loop, not just any loop in initialization or verification. A report may explain an alias check, a dependency or a cost-model decision. Preserve the compiler version and target flags alongside the report.

Start with a simple counted loop over contiguous memory and move unrelated work out of it. Function calls, early exits, unpredictable accesses and loop-carried dependencies can complicate vectorization. Intrinsics can provide control but tie code to an ISA and introduce alignment, dispatch and maintenance concerns. Compiler reports offer a useful first step before hand-writing architecture-specific code. An optimization report is evidence of a transformation, not a timing result.
lessons.pitfall: An aggressive target flag can create binaries that fail on older processors. Record the target and keep deployment compatibility explicit.

lessons.title: Remainders and promises
paragraphs: If N=19 and the model width is 4, there are four full groups and three remaining elements. A scalar cleanup loop processes the tail; another implementation might use a masked vector. The skip-tail setting deliberately leaves those outputs wrong so you can see why testing only N=16 misses the bug. Include N=1, N=width-1, N=width and N=width+1 in a test suite.

In C, restrict is a promise about how memory is accessed through pointers; it is not a request to ignore actual overlap. Standard C++17 has no restrict keyword, though compilers offer extensions. Alignment annotations are promises too. The native examples allocate separate buffers and let the compiler decide how to handle alignment, avoiding unsupported guarantees. If you add intrinsics or annotations, validate those preconditions at the API boundary.
lessons.pitfall: A false no-alias or alignment promise can make optimized code incorrect even when an unoptimized run appeared to work.

lessons.title: Dependencies, reductions and arithmetic changes
paragraphs: A sum reduction has a loop-carried dependency, whereas AXPY has independent element outputs. A compiler may need a different strategy or relaxed floating-point rules to transform a reduction. Multiple accumulators change addition order. Fused multiply-add can change rounding because it rounds once instead of rounding a multiplication and then an addition. Decide which differences your numerical contract permits.

Use compiler optimization independently from correctness instrumentation: first validate, then build a release executable and inspect reports. Compare every AXPY output, including the tail. For a more realistic experiment, use non-integer inputs with a mixed tolerance and explicitly control floating-point options. The course does not require fast-math; measuring a faster result is useful only when it still meets the required semantics.
lessons.pitfall: The browser’s skip-tail example demonstrates a logic error. A successful SIMD report cannot repair such an error.

courses.title: 6. OpenMP threads, races and reductions
courses.summary: Parallelize a numerical loop with explicit data sharing. Understand lost updates, atomics, private reductions and why a native data race has no reliable numerical meaning.
outcomes: Identify shared and private data in a parallel loop.
Choose a reduction or atomic operation for an accumulation.
Test thread-count independence and recognize false sharing.

lessons.title: Shared memory and work ownership
paragraphs: OpenMP adds a parallel programming model to C/C++ through directives and runtime calls. A parallel region forms a team; a worksharing for distributes loop iterations among that team. Threads share the process’s address space, but each thread has its own local execution state. Decide who writes each location. Independent output indices are often easy to distribute; a shared scalar update needs coordination.

The native sample uses parallel for with default(none), shared(n), and a reduction clause for the sum. The loop index has the required private behavior. Explicit sharing clauses make intent reviewable, but they do not automatically prove an algorithm correct. Compile and link with an OpenMP runtime; a build that ignores the pragma can silently remain serial. Run several thread counts and inspect the runtime configuration.
lessons.pitfall: An OpenMP-enabled compiler and runtime are needed. Adding a pragma to an arbitrary browser editor does not create native threads.

lessons.title: Read-modify-write is not one indivisible step
paragraphs: The expression sum += 1 conceptually reads a value, computes a new value, and writes it. Two workers can both read the same old value and overwrite each other’s updates if synchronization is missing. The browser’s unsafe-shared trace makes every worker read before any worker writes in each round. With four workers and ten rounds it ends at ten rather than forty, demonstrating lost updates.

In an actual C/C++ program, concurrent conflicting non-atomic accesses without the required synchronization create a data race and undefined behavior. The numerical result is not limited to the browser’s chosen interleaving. A run that happens to produce forty does not make that source safe. The native companion therefore contains only synchronized variants; the unsafe case is explored in a bounded trace rather than executed as supposedly meaningful native arithmetic.
lessons.pitfall: volatile is not a replacement for atomic operations, a lock, or an OpenMP reduction.

lessons.title: Private reductions versus atomics
paragraphs: A reduction gives workers private partial values and combines them using the declared operation. For addition, each private accumulator starts at the additive identity. This avoids contending on a shared sum every iteration. The alternative atomic update serializes access to the shared scalar at the required memory operation. Both are correct for the bounded integer sum in this example, but their synchronization frequency differs.

For floating-point addition, a reduction may combine partials in a different order from the serial loop. OpenMP does not promise a bitwise-identical addition tree across every execution. If exact reproducibility matters, choose and document an appropriate algorithm rather than assuming parallel sums are numerically interchangeable. For the native integer example, use a wide enough type so no intermediate or final sum overflows.
lessons.pitfall: A reduction is not a general fix for arbitrary dependencies between neighboring loop iterations.

lessons.title: Thread counts, false sharing and runtime costs
paragraphs: Test one, two and four threads, odd input sizes, and a size smaller than the thread count. Compare each synchronized result with n*(n+1)/2 computed in a sufficiently wide type. Keep thread creation and runtime initialization inside or outside the timing scope consistently. OMP_NUM_THREADS requests a team size, but runtime settings and resource limits can affect what is used; record the observed configuration when benchmarking.

False sharing occurs when threads update different logical values that occupy the same coherence line. It can cause expensive ownership movement without being a data race. Keeping partial accumulators local and writing them less often may help. Padding is a hypothesis to measure, not a portable 64-byte rule; line size and layout vary. Also avoid oversubscribing a host simply because more threads are available to request.
lessons.pitfall: A correct multithreaded result can be slower than a serial one when work is too small or synchronization dominates.

courses.title: 7. Scheduling, load balance and locality
courses.summary: Distribute uneven work with static blocks, cyclic chunks and dynamic scheduling. Balance useful work against dispatch cost, locality and thread placement.
outcomes: Explain why equal iteration counts need not mean equal work.
Compare static and dynamic scheduling using a visible task assignment.
Investigate false sharing, affinity and first-touch placement on a native host.

lessons.title: Count work rather than iterations
paragraphs: Iterations may have unequal cost. A particle near a dense region, an image tile with many features, or an adaptive solver cell can take more work than its neighbors. Dividing iterations equally then leaves some workers idle while the busiest worker finishes. The browser’s heavy-tail dataset makes the first three quarters of tasks cost one model unit and the remaining tasks cost sixteen units, so the imbalance is inspectable.

Completion time is determined by the most heavily loaded worker when there is no overlap with other phases. Total useful work stays constant across schedules. The lab shows both the sum of useful cost and the maximum worker completion time, plus a bar for each worker. It charges a declared dispatch cost to the worker receiving each chunk. This is a simplified scheduler model; it does not reproduce an operating-system scheduler or the OpenMP implementation’s central queue.
lessons.pitfall: Equal numbers of tasks per worker can still produce very unequal completion times.

lessons.title: Static blocks, cyclic chunks and dynamic assignment
paragraphs: Static-block gives each worker a contiguous portion. It has predictable ownership and often good locality when work per element is uniform. Static-cyclic distributes fixed-size chunks round-robin, spreading a clustered expensive region across workers while keeping deterministic ownership. Dynamic scheduling gives the next chunk to a worker that becomes available; it can adapt to irregular costs but adds dispatch and may weaken locality.

In OpenMP, schedule(runtime) allows the environment variable OMP_SCHEDULE to choose a policy without recompiling this example. Try static, static,1 and dynamic,1. The native runtime determines its actual schedule; the browser defines its own exact block and tie-breaking rules so its assignments can be reproduced. Do not demand that a native dynamic run match the browser’s worker-by-worker mapping. Compare correctness and broad effects on load and timing.
lessons.pitfall: Dynamic scheduling is not automatically best; uniform tiny tasks may spend more on dispatch than they save in balance.

lessons.title: Chunk size, cache lines and NUMA placement
paragraphs: Smaller chunks let idle workers acquire work sooner but increase the number of dispatches. Larger chunks amortize that cost and may preserve contiguous memory access, but one large expensive chunk can become a bottleneck. Sweep chunk sizes while holding the useful workload fixed. The model lets you change dispatch cost to see how the preferred choice can reverse. Task assignment should be a measured design decision, not a default copied into every loop.

On native systems, placement adds another dimension. OMP_PROC_BIND and OMP_PLACES can control affinity where supported. On NUMA machines, memory pages may be physically closer to one socket; initializing pages using the same ownership pattern as computation can improve first-touch placement. Cyclic writes can also put different workers on neighboring values in one coherence line. Verify topology and runtime behavior; these details are not represented by the browser’s cost bars.
lessons.pitfall: Changing affinity, chunk size and data layout together makes the resulting benchmark difficult to explain.

lessons.title: Correctness before scheduling claims
paragraphs: The native companion assigns every output element independently. It records the worker id for each task and verifies each value against a serial reference after the parallel loop completes. The artificial task performs repeated square roots, with extra iterations near the end, so it has actual uneven computational work. Worker counts show ownership, not the exact time spent per worker.

Run several samples for each policy at the same requested thread count. Keep runtime initialization and thread creation scope consistent and print or record the OpenMP environment. A schedule that is faster for the synthetic heavy tail may be worse for a real memory-bound kernel. Use the sandbox to develop a hypothesis, then measure a representative workload and retain the numerical oracle when changing its schedule.
lessons.pitfall: If two iterations write the same output unsafely, changing the schedule cannot make the program reliably correct.

formulas.symbols: P is worker count; work and time use the same modeled cost units.
formulas.assumptions: Costs are additive; each task executes exactly once; dispatch contributes time but not useful work.
formulas.example: Useful work 96, four workers and a makespan of 32 give U=75%.

formulas.symbols: N is task count; C is chunk size.
formulas.assumptions: Applies to cyclic/dynamic fixed chunks; static-block uses at most one block per active worker here.
formulas.example: For 24 tasks and chunk size 4, there are 6 dispatches.

courses.title: 8. Scaling, Roofline and accelerator decisions
courses.summary: Use Amdahl’s law and a resource ceiling to choose the next experiment. Separate strong scaling, weak scaling, logical traffic and measured bandwidth.
outcomes: Calculate speedup and parallel efficiency with stated assumptions.
Use arithmetic intensity to identify a resource-bound hypothesis.
Explain transfer costs and when a CPU/GPU comparison is fair.

lessons.title: Strong and weak scaling
paragraphs: Strong scaling holds total problem size fixed and increases workers. It asks how much sooner the same answer is available. Weak scaling grows the problem with the number of workers so useful work per worker stays approximately constant. It asks whether the system handles a larger total problem in similar time. Keep the two protocols separate: a larger workload finishing at the same time is not a strong-scaling speedup.

Amdahl’s simple fixed-work model divides baseline time into a serial fraction and a perfectly parallel fraction. Even an unlimited number of workers cannot remove the serial part. The explorer optionally adds overhead as a fraction of the one-worker baseline; it holds that entered overhead constant across the displayed rows to make the assumption explicit. Real overhead often changes with worker count and workload, so fit a model to evidence rather than treating the slider as a hardware forecast.
lessons.pitfall: More workers can reduce parallel work time while increasing communication, contention or synchronization enough to make the total slower.

lessons.title: Arithmetic intensity and a resource ceiling
paragraphs: Arithmetic intensity is useful FLOPs divided by bytes transferred at a specified memory level. Combining an attainable compute ceiling and attainable bandwidth gives a Roofline bound: performance cannot exceed either compute capacity or bandwidth times intensity under that model. The ridge point is where those limits meet. Below it, investigate traffic and reuse; above it, investigate compute efficiency and other limits. A bound is not a promise of achieved throughput.

The browser accepts assumed GB/s, GFLOP/s and FLOP/byte values in compatible decimal units. It reports a ceiling and the ridge, separately from the Amdahl result. It does not multiply them to invent a predicted application rate. A measured dot on a real Roofline plot requires measured time and a defensible operation/traffic count. Cache-level intensity differs from DRAM-level intensity, so label the level and keep both sides of the ratio consistent.
lessons.pitfall: Counting source-level loads as DRAM bytes can overcount cache reuse or miss write-allocation traffic.

lessons.title: Measure a simple bandwidth-heavy kernel
paragraphs: The native companion computes out=2*x+y with OpenMP, checks all outputs, and reports measured kernel time. It counts two logical FLOPs and 24 logical bytes per double element: two loads and one store. That logical arithmetic intensity is 1/12 FLOP per byte. The reported logical_GB_s is useful algorithmic traffic divided by time; it is deliberately not labeled a hardware-counter measurement of DRAM bandwidth.

Run the same N with one, two and four threads, retain repeated samples and state the warm-up policy. A small array may fit in cache; a large array may reach a memory-bandwidth plateau before all cores are useful. A timer reading below resolution is reported as unavailable, and you should increase N. Sanitizer runs help check memory behavior but should be separate from release performance data.
lessons.pitfall: The biggest FLOP/s number can come from a changed workload or precision. Keep the output contract and operation count visible.

lessons.title: NUMA, accelerators and end-to-end cost
paragraphs: A GPU offers many parallel execution resources, but offloading introduces allocation, transfer, launch and synchronization costs. A GPU kernel benchmark may omit transfers when data stays resident across many steps; an application benchmark must include transfers that the application actually performs. For asynchronous execution, synchronize the work before stopping an elapsed timer. Otherwise you may time only a queue submission. This path’s native programs execute on CPUs; the browser does not provide a CUDA or GPU runtime.

Consider offload when the problem exposes substantial parallel work and enough reuse or arithmetic to amortize movement. Keep large data resident where possible, batch useful work, and compare the complete pipeline with a checked CPU reference. On multi-socket CPUs, first-touch and affinity can change which bandwidth is available. On clusters, communication may dominate. Use these models to decide whether to study vectorization, locality, more CPU workers, communication, or a separate verified accelerator implementation.
lessons.pitfall: A GPU kernel speedup alone does not establish an end-to-end application speedup.

formulas.title: Amdahl with explicit overhead

formulas.assumptions: Fixed useful work; perfect parallel scaling of the nonserial part; entered overhead held constant.

formulas.symbols: Rpeak is GFLOP/s, B is GB/s, I is FLOP/byte.
formulas.assumptions: Both bandwidth and byte count refer to the same memory level; this is an upper bound.
formulas.example: B=50 and I=0.25 give a 12.5 GFLOP/s bandwidth ceiling below a 200 GFLOP/s compute ceiling.

courses.title: 9. MPI: distributed memory and collectives
courses.summary: Partition uneven data across processes, scatter it with counts and displacements, reduce partial results, and measure the slowest rank’s elapsed work.
outcomes: Distinguish MPI process memory from OpenMP shared memory.
Cover all elements with balanced counts, including zero-count ranks.
Use collectives with matching signatures and a consistent call order.

lessons.title: Ranks, communicators and separate address spaces
paragraphs: MPI programs consist of processes, each with its own address space. A rank identifies a process within a communicator; it is not a CPU core id or a globally unique machine id. MPI_COMM_WORLD groups the launched processes in these examples. MPI_Init starts the MPI environment, Comm_rank and Comm_size discover the rank and group size, and MPI_Finalize ends MPI use. Every process runs main(), so guard root-only initialization and printing explicitly.

Compile using mpicc or mpicxx from the installed MPI implementation so the correct headers and libraries are used. The C++ program uses MPI’s C function interface with C++ containers; it does not depend on the removed legacy MPI C++ bindings. A local mpiexec -n 4 run exercises real MPI processes on one machine. It validates communication behavior but is not evidence of multi-node network performance.
lessons.pitfall: An ordinary pointer value from rank zero is not a valid way to name rank zero’s buffer from another process.

lessons.title: Counts, remainders and displacements
paragraphs: For N elements and P ranks, assign floor(N/P) elements to each rank and one extra element to the first N mod P ranks. A rank’s displacement is the number of earlier elements: rank*floor(N/P)+min(rank,N mod P). For N=17 and P=4, counts are 5,4,4,4 and displacements are 0,5,9,13. Each rank’s range starts at its displacement and contains count elements.

When P>N, some ranks own zero elements. They still participate in the collective sequence with count zero. The native example allocates at least one local slot so it can provide a valid buffer even for a zero count. The browser’s drop-remainder setting intentionally assigns only floor(N/P) per rank and exposes the missing tail. Test uneven sizes and fewer elements than ranks; divisible sizes alone conceal this defect.
lessons.pitfall: For Scatterv, displacements use units of the send datatype extent, not arbitrary byte counts.

lessons.title: Scatterv, Reduce and consistent participation
paragraphs: Rank zero initializes the global array. MPI_Scatterv distributes different counts using MPI_DOUBLE. Each rank computes a private local sum. MPI_Reduce combines one double from each rank with MPI_SUM and places the result on root. All ranks in the communicator participate in the same ordered collective calls, with compatible counts, datatypes, operations and root. A root-only if around an entire collective can leave other ranks waiting forever.

A collective is not a substitute for understanding data dependencies or buffer lifetimes. Complete a communication operation before reusing buffers that it still accesses; nonblocking operations require completion through their requests. For this blocking example, the communication has completed on return under the operation’s defined semantics. Reduction trees and algorithms are implementation choices, and floating-point sums may use a different order than a serial accumulation.
lessons.pitfall: Calling a reduction with MPI_INT while the buffer holds doubles is a datatype mismatch, not an optimization.

lessons.title: Measure a distributed phase and propagate failures
paragraphs: The companion uses a barrier before its timed scatter/compute/reduce phase. Each rank measures elapsed time using MPI_Wtime on that rank, then a separate MPI_Reduce with MPI_MAX reports the largest local elapsed duration. The clocks need not share an absolute epoch to compare local durations. This timing convention helps identify the slowest participant, but does not include launch or the entire application. State that scope.

Only root has the reduced numerical result, so root checks it against N*(N+1)/2 and broadcasts the failure flag before all ranks finalize. The program exits consistently on a numerical mismatch. The browser also shows an illustrative tree-latency term ceil(log2(P))*latency, but actual MPI implementations may select other collective algorithms. Use local runs for behavior and a configured multi-node allocation for network measurements.
lessons.pitfall: Timing rank zero alone can miss a bottleneck elsewhere; reporting a synthetic tree cost as measured MPI latency is equally misleading.

courses.title: 10. Capstone: a verified distributed stencil
courses.summary: Build a complete HPC experiment around a time-stepped stencil: boundaries, double buffering, halo exchange, full-output testing and an honest performance report.
outcomes: Implement a Jacobi-style update with explicit boundary conditions.
Exchange current halos without deadlocking or overwriting dependencies.
Deliver source, test evidence and reproducible scaling results.

lessons.title: Specify the stencil before parallelizing
paragraphs: The problem is a one-dimensional array with N interior cells and two fixed boundary cells. The left boundary is 100 and the right boundary is 0; all interior cells start at zero. At each step, an interior cell becomes the average of its old left neighbor, its old value and its old right neighbor. This is a three-point Jacobi-style smoothing recurrence. It illustrates a dependency pattern; it is not a calibrated physical heat solver.

All updates for step t+1 must read step t. Use two buffers or otherwise preserve the old values until every dependent update is finished. Updating in place from left to right changes the recurrence because later cells see already-updated neighbors. The native program keeps separate old/new buffers, copies completed interior values, and leaves global boundaries fixed. The browser computes an independent serial array alongside its partitioned result.
lessons.pitfall: A plausible-looking smooth curve can come from the wrong recurrence. Check exact problem definition and every output cell.

lessons.title: Partition ownership and fresh halos
paragraphs: Each rank owns a contiguous set of interior cells and two halo slots holding neighbor values just outside its local range. At the beginning of every step, exchange the edge interior values needed by neighboring ranks. For a partition count greater than one, an internal interface needs one value in each direction. The outermost boundary values remain fixed and are not overwritten by a nonexistent neighbor.

The browser’s stale-halo option captures neighbor values once and then reuses them, demonstrating why the one-step answer may pass while later steps drift. With N=17, four partitions and ten steps, information should move through interfaces over time. Reusing initial halos blocks that propagation. The browser permits empty partitions by skipping them; the native stencil instead documents and enforces P<=N so every communicating rank owns at least one interior cell.
lessons.pitfall: Different empty-partition policies are valid only when explicit. Never let a rank send a nonexistent interior element.

lessons.title: Matching communication without buffering assumptions
paragraphs: The native implementation uses two MPI_Sendrecv calls per step. One sends the leftmost interior value left and receives the right halo from the right; the other sends the rightmost interior value right and receives the left halo. Distinct tags separate directions, with matching peers and MPI_DOUBLE datatypes. MPI_PROC_NULL represents a missing neighbor and leaves the boundary buffer unchanged on a null receive.

Sendrecv avoids relying on eager buffering to make a sequence of blocking sends finish. A later extension could post nonblocking receives and sends, compute strictly interior cells, wait for requests, then compute boundary-adjacent cells. That extension must retain buffers until communication completes and prove that computation does not consume stale halos. Merely replacing function names with nonblocking calls does not guarantee overlap or a speedup.
lessons.pitfall: A program that works for small messages may deadlock for larger ones if it relies on undocumented buffering of blocking sends.

lessons.title: Deliver a testable performance report
paragraphs: Gather the final interior values to root and compare all cells against a serial reference after the same number of steps. Test one rank, an uneven decomposition, one step and many steps. Use a maximum absolute error tolerance of 1e-12 for this bounded recurrence, and reject non-finite results. The native program reports the maximum local elapsed time for the step loop, including halo exchange and interior copying, while gathering and reference verification occur afterward.

The final deliverable is a source file, exact build/run commands, environment description, test matrix, raw timings and a short explanation of the result. Compare strong scaling at fixed N and step count; optionally study weak scaling with stated growth. Explain when communication dominates and why a more complex optimization is justified. Keep practice and the exam separate from this evidence: a quiz score is a learning aid, not proof of native correctness or a cluster performance certification.
lessons.pitfall: A passed exam does not replace executing the edited program’s tests. Preserve both the numerical evidence and the measurement protocol.

formulas.assumptions: Every right-hand value comes from the previous step.

formulas.symbols: One double crosses each internal interface in each direction.
formulas.assumptions: One-dimensional nearest-neighbor partitioning; excludes protocol overhead and other collectives.
formulas.example: Four active partitions exchange 6 values, or 48 payload bytes, per step.

Gatherv reassembles the global interior. Root computes the serial recurrence independently, compares every cell, broadcasts failure and finalizes consistently.
